description: Getting things done not sure what yet but things
summary: S.G.U.F. is a wearable health-monitoring system that lets astronauts check their own health without medical training, while keeping Earth's flight surgeons informed. Our Arduino prototype reads pulse and movement, logs astronauts in with an RFID tag, and shows a green, amber or red traffic light plus a plain-language LCD message. A Raspberry Pi hub compares every reading with the astronaut's own baseline, and a crew app collects activity, posture and mood check-ins. Alerts are reassuring, jargon-free and automatically sent to Mission Control. A planned microneedle patch would track blood counts; blood and pressure data are simulated and clearly labelled. It addresses the challenge by reducing human error and mental load, flagging early changes linked to NASA's five spaceflight hazards, and telling crew when to contact a flight surgeon. Points for completing check-ups, never for health values, and mission leaderboards make routine monitoring engaging and support crew wellbeing.
details:
**What it does.** An astronaut puts on the wearable and taps their RFID tag to log in. Pulse and movement are read while a short questionnaire covers activity, posture, back and hip aches, and a 1 to 5 mood check-in. The habitat hub compares every reading with that astronaut's own first-week baseline, not a population average. The wrist light and LCD show green (normal), amber (check again) or red (contact the flight surgeon), and each message is written in calm, plain English, for example: "Your red blood cell count is a bit lower than usual. This is very common in spaceflight due to fluid shifts. Mission Control has automatically received these results and is reviewing them." A flight-surgeon dashboard on Earth receives the full detail, batched so it works over a Mars-style delayed link.

**How it works.** The wearable is an Arduino with a MAX30105 pulse sensor, MPU6050 IMU, MFRC522 RFID reader, a 16x2 I2C LCD, traffic-light LEDs and Bluetooth. A Raspberry Pi 5 hub stores readings in SQLite, runs the baseline comparison and scoring in Python, and serves a Streamlit crew app. Two simulated crew members, ABC (a normal week) and DEF (a worrying trend that turns amber), validate the alert logic; 307 automated checks in run_checks.py pass against both. A microneedle patch for a blood panel every two days is proposed and researched (materials, sterilisation, point-of-care blood counting) but not built; those values are simulated and labelled.

**Benefits and impact.** Not every astronaut is a doctor. S.G.U.F. removes the need to read raw numbers, minimises human error in reporting, and protects mental bandwidth by explaining results without medical jargon and without alarm. It tells the crew exactly when a flight surgeon needs to be involved. The points system rewards taking check-ups, never the health values, so nobody is penalised for a worrying reading, and a mission scoreboard normalised per day in space adds a team element that supports morale on long missions.

**NASA's five hazards.** Radiation: blood-count trend against the astronaut's own baseline (indicator only, not a dose). Isolation and confinement: mood check-in, points and scoreboard. Distance from Earth: decisions in the habitat, store-and-forward summaries to Earth. Gravity: posture and ache questions, movement and exercise minutes instead of steps. Closed environment: cabin temperature, humidity and pressure logged alongside sleep and mood.

**Tools.** Python 3.12 (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, pyserial, Pillow, Streamlit), Arduino C++ (MFRC522, SparkFun MAX3010x, Adafruit MPU6050, LiquidCrystal_I2C), SQLite, Raspberry Pi 5, static HTML/SVG and PNG for diagrams.

**Creativity and factors we considered.** We came at the problem from the astronaut's side: the hardest part of self-monitoring is not the sensor, it is understanding the result and staying calm. So every message was written to be reassuring and jargon-free, with Mission Control already in the loop. Our microbiologist wrote the on-screen explanations for each blood-count result from the biology, and our game developer designed the arcade-style scoreboard, which is our own design and borrows no game's name, art or characters. We kept hard rules throughout: every simulated value is labelled SIMULATED, skin temperature is skin surface only, mood is non-clinical, the blood-count trend is an exposure indicator and not a radiation dose, points never depend on health values, no real tag IDs are stored (salted hashes only), no NASA logos or mission identifiers are used, and the system is not medical advice.
